newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: More HK firms seek Singapore listing before 1997.
newsitem.headline: More HK firms seek Singapore listing before 1997.

text.p: The pace of Hong Kong companies seeking a listing on the Singapore exchange is expected to pick up this week and gather steady steam by the end of 1996, corporate finance bankers said.

Seafood processing group Pacific Andes is expected to start the ball rolling by launching a Singapore initial public offering in the middle of this week and more companies are expected to follow suit, said one corporate banker who declined to be named.
"My guess is that we could see up to six more Hong Kong listings before the year-end," the banker said.
So far, a total 15 Hong Kong firms have listed in Singapore, and the number is expected to increase with the authorities keen to promote Singapore as a regional bourse.

While Hong Kong companies seeking listings on the local exchange is not new, bankers said they note greater interest from such companies with less than 300 days before the British colony returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997.

"I don't think the companies will admit it but certainly 1997 is a factor," said Eu Mun Leong, vice president of corporate finance with United Overseas Bank. "And I expect the interest for listings here to continue."
"They are just hedging their positions," said Herbert Hui, deputy chief executive of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong on a recent visit to Singapore when asked to comment on the trend.
Hong Kong companies usually retain their listing status in the colony, normally under the parent holding company.
Pacific Andes is retaining its Hong Kong listing status while spinning off its seafood trading and processing arm for a listing in Singapore.

It will be the fourth Hong Kong company to list in Singapore this year. Others are toy maker Wah Sing International, shipping group Ming Wah Universal (Bermuda) Co and tile maker Interform Ceramics Technologies.
Eu said companies listing in Singapore were generally smaller industrial firms as the Hong Kong exchange seemed to favour large companies with exposure in property and banking.

"Smaller companies especially those engaged in trading and manufacturing are often neglected," said Eu, adding that such companies often found they could get a better price-earnings ratio in Singapore.
The fortunes of Hong Kong companies listed in Singapore have been mixed. Some have experienced hardly any after market interest in their shares, usually quoted in U.S. dollars.
Brokers have said investors find trading shares in a currency other than the Singapore dollar inconvenient.

"It is incovenient for investors but they are beginning to accept this," said Goh Yew Lin, managing director GK Goh Stockbrokers. "It really depends on the quality of the company. If the company is good, people will trade it even if it is in U.S. dollars. Just look at Jardine Matheson."

According to the latest Stock Exchange of Singapore journal, Jardine Matheson, Hongkong Land and GPE Industries were among the most active stocks in July with a combined turnover of about 80 million shares during the month.
"It very much depends on how much institutional interest there is in the company in the first place and also how the company tries to promote greater awareness among investors," said Eu.

Brokers noted that Pacific Andes, which recently began broadcasting a radio jingle for its seafood products in Singapore, appeared to be making the effort to lift its profile ahead of its debut on the local bourse.
